title: Round Table, No Neighbours
statement: Twelve knights sit around a round table. In how many ways can we choose a set of knights, possibly empty, so that no two chosen knights sit next to each other?
hints: First solve it for knights on a bench, in a line. You should see Fibonacci numbers.
At the round table, split on whether knight $1$ is chosen.
solution: For $n$ knights in a line the count is $F_{n+2}$ (Fibonacci, $F_1=F_2=1$). At the table, if knight $1$ is not chosen the other $11$ form a line: $F_{13} = 233$. If knight $1$ is chosen, knights $2$ and $12$ are out and knights $3$ to $11$ form a line of $9$: $F_{11} = 89$. Total $233 + 89 = 322$, the Lucas number $L_{12}$.
